analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal and state enforcement of wage, child labor, and workplace safety laws.
analysis.headline: A bill to expand federal and state labor law enforcement drew 65 cosponsors, including 2 Republicans, but never received a single committee hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Workers POWER Act would rebuild the Department of Labor's enforcement staff by adding paid student interns, doubling its Recent Graduates program, creating child labor investigator fellowships, expanding its honors attorney program, and adding bonuses and larger student loan repayment for enforcement staff. It would also send up to $250 million a year in grants to state labor departments to hire more investigators and clear case backlogs, with states required to share investigation data with the federal government. The stated goal is more enforcement of wage, child labor, and workplace safety laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are shorted on pay, children working illegally, and people hurt by unsafe workplaces, because more federal and state investigators means more inspections and recovered wages. Law-abiding employers also gain a more level playing field against competitors who cut costs through violations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing wage theft and unsafe conditions

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Labor Department to create at least five paid post-secondary student positions and two more interns in each regional office of the Wage and Hour Division, paying at least the GS-7 starting rate.

Doubles the number of Recent Graduates program positions at the Labor Department and creates at least five child labor fellowship positions each in the Wage and Hour Division and OSHA, with an option to convert fellows to career positions.
Expands the Department's honors attorney program to at least 20 positions, focused on building a pipeline of lawyers into wage-and-hour and safety enforcement.

Establishes performance, recruitment, relocation, and retention bonus programs for Wage and Hour Division and OSHA employees, including critical-skill incentives of up to 25% of pay for enforcement staff.
Raises student loan repayment for Department employees from $10,000 to $30,000 per year and from $60,000 to $180,000 lifetime, in exchange for a five-year service agreement.

Authorizes $250 million a year in competitive grants to state labor departments to recruit and retain enforcement staff, prioritizing states with the greatest need, with funds required to supplement rather than replace state spending.
Requires states receiving grants to share investigation data with the Labor Department, including locations of violations and entities that routinely violate labor laws.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayer money funds the new positions, bonuses, loan repayment, and up to $250 million a year in state grants. Businesses that violate wage, child labor, or safety laws pay through more investigations, back-wage recovery, and penalties.

drawbacks.text: Authorizes $250 million per year in state grant spending on top of the cost of new federal positions, bonuses, and loan repayment, with no offsetting cuts elsewhere in the bill.

Waives the standard federal certification and approval requirements for bonuses and allows critical-skill incentives up to 25% of an employee's pay, which loosens normal oversight of how the money is awarded.

Lets employees collect up to $180,000 in student loan repayment, and caps are only recoverable if the employee completes a five-year service agreement, a benefit critics could view as generous compared with private-sector norms.
States receiving grants must enter data-sharing agreements with the federal government, a condition some states might refuse, limiting the grant program's reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: wage theft, child labor, and safety violations are chronic, and enforcement depends on having enough investigators, which this bill would directly fund. The cost is modest relative to a $250 million annual grant program plus federal hiring, but the generous bonus and loan-repayment provisions for the agency's own staff are the weakest part of the design, and on balance the bill is a straightforward capacity investment rather than a giveaway to any industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on December 6, 2023 by Rep. Morgan McGarvey with 34 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor action afterward.
It accumulated 65 cosponsors, 63 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and all unfinished bills die when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who benefit from thin enforcement of wage, child labor, and safety laws are better off because the bill never moved, since more investigators and state funding never arrived. No taxpayer money was spent on the program.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers relying on weak labor enforcement

for.name: Morgan McGarvey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 34 original cosponsors.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred to her committee; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic: 63 of 65 cosponsors were Democrats, only 2 of 224 House Republicans signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee took no action.

industries.industry: Employers that violate wage, child labor, or workplace safety laws
industries.note: More federal investigators, child labor fellowships, and state grant funding mean more inspections, back-wage recovery, and penalties for wage theft, illegal child labor, and unsafe conditions. These employers profit by underpaying or endangering workers, so their interest runs against the people the bill protects.

industries.industry: State and local labor enforcement agencies
industries.note: Up to $250 million a year in grants would fund hiring and retention to clear backlogs, with funds required to supplement rather than replace state money. Their gain comes through doing more enforcement for workers.
Stronger enforcement of wage and hour rules levels the playing field against competitors who cut labor costs through violations.
